tagline: Red asphalt switchbacks climb between the cliffs of Zion’s northwest corner
intro: Kolob Fingers Road climbs through Zion’s northwest corner on red asphalt switchbacks. This five-mile Utah state scenic byway has two lanes, narrow shoulders and sharp curves. UDOT highlights its sandstone cliffs, narrow canyons and overlooks. The drive gains more than 1,000 feet; beside it, parallel box canyons cut into the Colorado Plateau’s western edge form cliff walls 2,000 feet high. UDOT allows 15 minutes each way for the drive, whose grades become steeper near the end.

Before that protection, Mormon settlers used the Kolob country for timber and grazing and diverted water to irrigate crops in the valley below. Kolob Canyons became a separate Zion National Monument in 1937 and joined Zion National Park in 1956. The five-mile road was built to give access to this section of the park. The canyons themselves are designated Wilderness, protected for their primitive environments.

Enter from I-15 at Exit 40 and begin at the visitor center. Beyond it, a sharp turn opens the view toward the Markagunt Plateau and Horse Ranch Mountain, Zion’s highest peak. The road curves past the box canyon of Taylor Creek’s south fork, then follows a ridgeline to the turnabout at Timber Creek Overlook.

moments.title: Kolob Canyons Visitor Center
moments.text: Near the present visitor center, Silvestre Vélez de Escalante and Francisco Atanasio Domínguez passed on October 13, 1776, the first people of European descent known to visit the area. Mormon settlers later used Kolob Canyons for timber and livestock grazing, and diverted its water to crops in the valley below. They named the area Kolob, the heavenly place nearest God’s residence in Mormon scripture. The visitor center now serves as the required pass or entrance-fee stop for the canyon road. Beyond the road, the Kolob Canyons district has more than twenty miles of hiking trails among Navajo sandstone peaks and canyon streams.

moments.title: Taylor Creek
moments.text: The road curves beside a box canyon carved by Taylor Creek’s south fork. Above the creek’s drainage, Paria Point is made of Jurassic Navajo sandstone resting on tilted layers of the Kayenta Formation. Paria Point and its neighbors are separated by finger canyons 2,000 feet deep. Beyond the park boundary, the 32-acre Taylor Creek Wilderness protects the creek’s upper headwaters. Designated in 2009, that adjoining wilderness connects the canyon’s story to the water feeding the Virgin River system. Water running off Paria Point reaches Taylor Creek and belongs to the Virgin River drainage basin.

moments.title: Timber Creek Overlook
moments.text: The drive ends at a turnabout on the ridgeline, after climbing more than 1,000 feet. Timber Creek Overlook has views of the Kolob Terrace and the Pine Valley Mountains. UDOT records the road’s ending elevation as 6,234 feet and describes steeper grades near its end. A short hiking trail and picnic area also serve Timber Creek.

practical: Kolob Canyons Visitor Center: Stop at the visitor center to show an Interagency Park Pass or pay the park entrance fee. The road may close in winter because of snow or ice. (checked 2026-10-11)
